reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents as a limbic encephalitis with early, frequently prominent and refractory seizures
Subacute memory impairment, confusion, and behavioural change accompany the seizures
Antibodies target the B1 subunit of the metabotropic GABA-B receptor
Has a strong paraneoplastic association, most often with small-cell lung carcinoma, so thoracic imaging and tumour screening are essential
Coexisting antibodies to other onconeural or surface antigens are not uncommon and may modify the phenotype
MRI typically shows medial temporal signal change consistent with limbic encephalitis
Management pairs seizure control and immunotherapy (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab) with treatment of any underlying tumour
reference.pathophysiology: Antibodies are directed against the B1 subunit of the metabotropic gamma-aminobutyric acid type B (GABA-B) receptor, which mediates slow inhibitory neurotransmission. Impaired GABA-B signalling reduces inhibition within limbic and cortical circuits, lowering seizure threshold and disrupting memory networks. The disorder is frequently paraneoplastic, with an immune response cross-reacting with receptor expressed by an underlying tumour, most commonly small-cell lung carcinoma; identification and treatment of that tumour is central to management.
additionalDifferentials: Other autoimmune limbic encephalitides (LGI1, NMDA receptor, AMPA receptor)
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid testing for GABA-B receptor antibodies and a wider autoimmune panel
MRI of the brain to demonstrate limbic involvement
Electroencephalography to characterise seizures and subclinical activity
CT of the chest and whole-body imaging to detect small-cell lung carcinoma
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for inflammation and to exclude infection
redFlags: Evidence of an underlying malignancy requiring urgent oncological input
reference.prognosis: Seizures and cognition often improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but outcome is heavily influenced by the underlying malignancy, and paraneoplastic cases carry a more guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Failing to search thoroughly for small-cell lung carcinoma
Overlooking coexisting antibodies that alter management
Assuming a benign course when the disorder is paraneoplastic
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Prompt first-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Escalation to second-line immunotherapy such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide in refractory or relapsing disease
Diligent search for and treatment of an underlying tumour, most often small-cell lung carcinoma, as tumour treatment is central to disease control
Control of the frequently refractory seizures with antiseizure medications, escalating to intensive care management for status epilepticus
Supportive and rehabilitative care for the cognitive and behavioural impairment
Ongoing surveillance for tumour recurrence and neurological relapse
Multidisciplinary care coordinated between neurology and oncology
